w: One of Utrecht's medieval parish churches, the Jacobikerk still sends pilgrims on their way - it's the traditional starting point for the Dutch heading out on the Way of St James toward Santiago de Compostela, with the Dutch Confraternity of St James still keeping an office just round the corner.
s: Where Dutch pilgrims to Santiago still set off
_facts: Landmark Protestant church on St Jacobsstraat, named for St James the Greater
One of Utrecht's medieval parish churches, alongside the Buurkerk, Nikolaikerk and Geertekerk
Known today as the starting place for Dutch pilgrims on the Way of St James to Santiago de Compostela
The Dutch Confraternity of St James is located around the corner on St Jacobskerkhof

w: Tucked just off the Dom's shadow, this gothic-revival church is run by the traditionalist Society of Saint Pius X, saying the old Latin Mass inside a nineteenth-century building most visitors walk straight past. Locals call it a hidden treasure, and the Maarschalkerweerd organ inside is reason enough to duck in.
s: A hidden gothic-revival church steps from the Dom
_facts: Roman Catholic church at Minrebroederstraat 21, operated by the Society of Saint Pius X (SSPX), dedicated to Saint Willibrord
A rijksmonument since 1976, near the Dom Church in the historical centre
Considered a hidden treasure and a fine example of Dutch gothic revival, built in the 19th century
Has a well-known organ built by Maarschalkerweerd

w: Dug to link Utrecht to the Lek and, through it, the whole Rhine shipping network, the Vaartse Rijn was once the working canal that kept the city's trade moving before the roads took over. Quieter now, it still traces the old route south out of the centre toward Nieuwegein.
s: The old working canal that once fed Utrecht's trade
_facts: Canal connecting Utrecht with Nieuwegein and the Lek river in the province of Utrecht
Formerly a major shipping route between Utrecht and the Rhine basin

w: By 1580, this was the second-oldest monastery left standing in the Netherlands, beaten only by Egmond Abbey to the north. Centuries of monastic life in the heart of Utrecht, now reduced to a name and a footprint in the old city - a quiet reminder of how thoroughly the Reformation reshaped this town.
_facts: In 1580 it was the second-oldest monastery in the Netherlands, second only to Egmond Abbey

w: Utrecht's signature trick: wharves built right at water level, with dry cellars underneath reachable straight from the canal - locked in place by 1275 once the city's locks made the water level constant. Merchants once unloaded barges into these werven; today the old cellars are restaurants and cafes.
s: The canal that gave Utrecht its underground wharf cellars
_facts: The 'old canal' running through the centre of Utrecht, with a northern section dating to around AD 1000 and a southern section begun in 1122
The city's lock system, finished in 1275, kept the water level constant, enabling permanently dry cellars and quays at water level (werven)
Warehouses once lined the canal; many are now restaurants and cafes
